entries.name: companion-identity-not-derived-from-the-source
entries.claim: The companion transaction and line identities are a pure function of the stock-count source record ids. Deriving them from anything else -- here, from fresh randomness -- means the kernel mints a companion identity nothing can recompute, which is exactly the `#companionDerivation` copies-rather-than-derives defect `purchasing-sales-v1-plan.md` section 7.16 measured. Scope of this entry's evidence: the kill set is measured within the three `companion derivation` tests this command runs, which is what the runner observes; the mutation also reds the wider stock-count file, and that is stated rather than measured here.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: a source with no pre-staged transaction posts and the kernel writes both companion identities
kills.expected: does not carry the derived companion transaction identity

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: the companion transaction and its lines are the kernel projection of the count
kills.expected: does not carry the derived companion transaction identity

entries.name: companion-revision-left-at-the-column-default
entries.claim: The kernel WRITES the companion transaction's revision, derived as sourceRevision + 1, rather than letting the column default supply it. Both companions of one posting carry the same derived revision, so a reader can join a posted count to its companion and see one consistent pair; a companion left at the default disagrees with the source it projects.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: a source with no pre-staged transaction posts and the kernel writes both companion identities
kills.expected: does not carry the derived companion transaction identity

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: the companion transaction and its lines are the kernel projection of the count
kills.expected: does not carry the derived companion transaction identity

entries.name: source-companion-column-never-written
entries.claim: The posted transition is where the source's companion transaction identity is written. Dropping that one assignment leaves a posted stock count whose companion column is still null -- the source posts, the movements land, and nothing records which transaction they belong to. That is the silent-until-reconciled failure this packet's Band A declaration is about.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: a source with no pre-staged transaction posts and the kernel writes both companion identities
kills.expected: does not carry the derived companion transaction identity

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: the companion transaction and its lines are the kernel projection of the count
kills.expected: does not carry the derived companion transaction identity

entries.name: source-line-companion-column-never-written
entries.claim: Line-level companion identity is written per source line, not implied by the header. Writing null instead still satisfies the update's own row count -- the guard is `IS NULL` and the row stays null -- so only the read-back catches it. This is the vacuity vector where a write reports success and the fact does not hold.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: a source with no pre-staged transaction posts and the kernel writes both companion identities
kills.expected: lines do not all carry a derived companion line identity

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: the companion transaction and its lines are the kernel projection of the count
kills.expected: lines do not all carry a derived companion line identity

entries.name: reviewed-source-companion-must-be-null-fence-removed
entries.claim: The kernel is the ONLY writer of a companion identity, so a reviewed stock count must not already name one. Replacing the fence with whatever is stored makes the kernel adopt a companion transaction written by something else. This is the packet's gate-invisible deliverable -- an operator-visible refusal the binding makes possible -- and it dies alone: the two posting tests are unaffected because their stored value is null either way.
entries.original:
const expectedCompanionId =
    state === binding.stockCountReviewedState ? null : command.transactionId;

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: a reviewed count that already names a companion transaction is refused
kills.expected: a reviewed count carrying a companion identity the kernel did not write must be refused

entries.name: family-roster-transaction-type-repointed
entries.claim: The companion transaction's type comes from the compiled family roster's role binding, not from a switch arm. Repointing the count role's declared transaction type in the roster changes what the kernel writes, which is what makes the roster load-bearing rather than decorative. It dies alone: only the projection test reads the companion's type.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: the companion transaction and its lines are the kernel projection of the count
kills.expected: the companion type comes from the family role binding

entries.name: companion-business-key-not-derived-from-identity
entries.claim: The companion transaction's business key is derived from the derived identity, so it is unique whenever the identity is. A fixed number makes every companion in a tenant collide on `inventory_transaction_number`'s case-insensitive unique business key -- the first posting looks correct and the second refuses, which is why a single-posting test must observe the number itself rather than the absence of a collision.

kills.name: stock-count companion derivation: the companion transaction and its lines are the kernel projection of the count
kills.expected: the companion business key must be derived from the companion identity
